official_name: Neurocognitive Disorder Due to Huntington's Disease
plain_title: Thinking and mood changes in an inherited brain condition
one_liner: Thinking decline and mood changes caused by Huntington's disease, an inherited condition that also affects movement.
in_simple_words: Huntington's disease is a rare, inherited condition caused by a single gene; each child of a parent with it has a 50% chance of inheriting it. It usually begins between 30 and 50 and progresses over 15 to 20 years, affecting movement (jerky movements, clumsiness), thinking (planning, slowed processing), and mood (depression, irritability, apathy). Thinking and mood changes often come before movement problems. There's no cure, but symptoms can be treated and families can be supported, including with genetic counselling.
what_it_can_feel_like: I watched it take my mother. Then I had the test. Knowing changed how I live, not whether I live.
The irritability came years before the movements. We blamed stress.
HDSA connected us with families who'd walked this road. That mattered more than any drug.
common_signs: Family history of Huntington's disease; positive genetic test
Slowed thinking, trouble planning, organizing, and switching tasks
Depression, irritability, apathy, anxiety, or obsessive thinking
Involuntary jerky movements, clumsiness, or restlessness
Onset usually between 30 and 50; gradual progression
Thinking and mood changes often preceding movement symptoms

myths_vs_facts.myth: Huntington's is only a movement disorder.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Thinking and mood changes are core features and often appear first. Depression and suicide risk are serious concerns.

myths_vs_facts.myth: If I have the gene, there's no point planning anything.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Many people live decades after diagnosis. Planning, treatment, and support shape those years, and research is advancing.

myths_vs_facts.myth: Everyone at risk should get tested.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Testing is a personal choice made with genetic counselling. Many at-risk people choose not to test, and that's valid.

how_common.plain: Huntington's disease is rare, affecting roughly 5 to 10 people in every 100,000 in populations of European descent, with lower rates elsewhere.
how_common.figure: About 5–10 per 100,000 in European-origin populations; lower in Asian and African populations (reviews)

what_helps.plain_summary: Care is multidisciplinary: neurologists, psychiatrists, therapists, dietitians, and social workers. Medications prescribed and monitored by a doctor can ease involuntary movements, depression, irritability, and other symptoms. Physiotherapy, speech therapy, occupational therapy, and nutrition support function. Genetic counselling supports families and at-risk relatives. Specialist HD clinics and organizations provide expertise, and planning for care and finances early makes a difference.
evidence_based_options: Specialist HD clinic and multidisciplinary care
Medication for movement, mood, and behavioural symptoms, prescribed and monitored by a doctor
Physiotherapy, speech, occupational therapy, and nutrition support
Genetic counselling; carer and family support
self_help_that_supports_care: Routines and a calm, predictable environment
Staying active and eating enough, as HD burns a lot of energy
Talking about mood changes early; depression is treatable
HD organizations and groups for the person, carers, and at-risk relatives

when_to_reach_out: If you have a family history of Huntington's and notice mood, thinking, or movement changes, contact a doctor or HD clinic. For questions about testing, ask for genetic counselling. If you're feeling hopeless or thinking of ending your life, use the crisis strip now; depression in HD is treatable.
is_not: Other movement disorders and dementias can look similar; a genetic test confirms Huntington's. Depression or anxiety in an at-risk person doesn't mean the disease has started.
hope_note: Families with Huntington's are among the most resilient communities in medicine, and research toward treatments that slow the disease is moving faster than ever.

content_notes: Site-wide crisis link stays one tap away.
Suicide risk is raised in HD; the 'when to reach out' text names this and the crisis strip applies via the chapter rule.
